claims.text: Introducing a moderate amount of aluminum into a refractory high-entropy alloy will significantly improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
Bulk aluminum alloying and surface aluminization are alternative interventions capable of producing the proposed oxidation benefit.
The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy forms a noncoherent or porous oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
A sufficient optimized aluminum concentration will induce selective oxidation and formation of an adherent alumina scale.
The aluminum intervention should work during exposure at approximately 1100°C in air containing 21% oxygen for 100 hours.
The aluminum intervention produces a coherent, dense Al2O3 layer on the alloy surface.
Aluminum preferentially oxidizes to form Al2O3.
Al2O3 is thermodynamically stable and slow-growing under the proposed conditions.
The alumina scale acts as an oxygen-diffusion barrier and reduces further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
Compared with the untreated alloy, the aluminum-modified alloy will develop a thinner oxide scale.
Compared with the untreated alloy, the aluminum-modified alloy will develop a more adherent oxide scale.
Compared with the untreated alloy, the aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit lower weight gain and a lower oxidation rate.
The untreated alloy's less-protective oxide permits greater oxygen penetration and more rapid scale thickening.
The protective effect should remain robust in air up to about 1200°C.
At temperatures significantly above 1200°C, scale spallation or accelerated oxidation kinetics may undermine the benefit.
